title: Graphics Lab, a technical record
summary: The rendering and simulation experiments behind the homepage's coastal home, one technique at a time: what each does in the scene now and which files and functions hold it, the papers it adapts, what it cannot do yet, and newer papers that would take it further, each with what it would add and a rough effort. A performance system records where the frame goes, what was cut on October 18, 2026, and the next techniques to try in priority order.
scope: Each experiment adapts a published method in a small, bounded form for a browser scene, and each entry says where it simplifies. Thumbnails are frames of the live scene captured on October 18, 2026, after the renovation and the skinned wildlife, with the scene's clock set to Friday, October 16; the light well, the steam and the onsen are dated in late August, when the noon sun reaches the shaft and the bath runs in daylight. Measurements come from one shared Windows laptop (Intel Core Ultra 7 155H with Arc integrated graphics) unless an entry says otherwise. Shader warmup and loading are in the coastal home record.
credit: Compiled on October 16 to 18, 2026 by Anthropic's Claude from the code, the scene notes and the coastal home record, for Sirui Tao to review. The performance system and the renovation's surfaces joined on October 18 from entries the agents who built them prepared and checked. Every citation was checked against its DOI record, its publisher's page or its authors' page.

read_first.why: The coastal home record. Each technique's full implementation notes, its design moves and the house's constraints.
The active brief. The 2D-first rule, the San Diego routine and the acceptance evidence map.
The ocean, the coast's wind, the record mechanics and the curtains, with equations, sources, evidence and limits.
The horizon integral, its reconstruction and the controlled comparisons.
The height-field pool, its hand coupling and its numerical evidence.
The curved-patch diffusion integral, metric curvature and the exact shader hook.
Steam transport, light integration around glass and the light-well mask.
The traced sky and lamp bounce, its probes and its cost.
The curl field, leaf attachment and particle integration.
How to measure the frame, what was cut on October 18, the rules for later work and the next techniques to try.

constraints: The homepage opens in 2D on every screen, 3D loads only on request, and any WebGL or model failure returns the 2D desk. No experiment may change that.
Every simulation advances on the scene's active clock in fixed ticks, accepts at most 0.25 s per call and drops the rest. Paused, hidden, offscreen and reduced-motion scenes compose a still frame.
Every new material, pass or override draw joins `program-warmup.mjs`, or its first draw blocks the page.
A change meant only to save cost must change 0 pixels in seeded, paused-clock captures; a change of look needs a matched A/B, measured interleaved.
The scene renders through WebGL2 and three.js r164, with no compute shaders and no ray queries; GPU work is vertex and fragment passes.
Store any array-of-vectors uniform as a flat `Float32Array`, and give a caster animated only in its vertex shader its own depth material, or the shadow cache keeps its shadow in place.
Each technique's notes say where it simplifies the paper it adapts. Never present an adaptation as a full reproduction or as the state of the art.

tests.covers: This record's schema, paths, named functions, links to the coastal home record, sources and watchlists.
The light lab's optics against Fresnel and Snell, its water hits, and agreement between the two estimators.
Wave derivatives, slope-energy accounting, water Fresnel and La Jolla's sun.
The coast's breeze against the station means, its gust fronts, the wind sea and the planting's sway.
Conservation, reflecting boundaries, energy decay and the hand's coupling in the pool.
Steam transport across frame rates, positive diffusion and Beer–Lambert composition.
Cloth strain, stability, determinism, sleep and wake, and the openness model.
The diffusion integral's normalization, limits and curvature.
The lifts' reach, contacts and head clearances on every avatar.
Which casters the shadow cache keeps, what redraws it, and the cases that keep three's own shadow path.
Nonblank WebGL, the rooms, recovery and reduced motion in a real browser.

systems.name: Light
systems.summary: Light that has to be traced rather than rasterized: down a drilled shaft, around the house's walls, into the creases where things touch, and through rippled water in a lab page of its own.

techniques.name: Light paths through the onsen

thumbnail.alt: The lab's onsen rendered twice, specks of path tracing on the left and Metropolis light transport's sunlit pool floor on the right
thumbnail.frame: The lab's eleven-minute comparison at 800 × 600, scaled.

techniques.what: A plain-JavaScript renderer races path tracing against Metropolis light transport on the sunlight the light well bends through the onsen's water.
techniques.how: `createRenderer` in `core.mjs` builds one path sampler that reads every random decision from a fixed coordinate of a sample vector. `PathTracer` feeds it fresh numbers and `MetropolisRenderer` feeds it Kelemen and colleagues' small and large mutations, so the two estimators share every line of path construction. Both use next-event estimation to the sun and sky with power-heuristic multiple importance sampling, after Veach, and water hits use safeguarded Newton iteration on seven frozen ripples. The page runs each estimator in a module worker for the same wall time, and `make_light_lab_reference.mjs` splits path space at the first hit for a 24-minute reference.

files.role: The scene, the path sampler and both estimators.
One estimator per worker.
The race, its chart and the still frames.
The reference renderer, split by path type.

limits: A simplified scene. A box grotto, frozen ripples, no steam, a round opening instead of the tilted shaft, and a sun three times its real size by default.
Metropolis takes its total brightness from independent samples that usually miss the sun, and its chains start in skylight.

watchlist.adds: Solves for the path through the water from a point on the pool floor to the sun, so even plain path tracing could aim at the sun. The lab's pool has a single refracting surface, the method's simplest case.
Integrates the light arriving through each facet of a triangulated water surface in closed form, a next-event estimator for caustics under water.
Moves a chain along the family of paths that stay connected through the water instead of hoping a random change does, so the race's caustic paths would mix much faster.
Learns which directions reach the sun from each region and samples them, an unbiased alternative to Metropolis whose independent samples also give the image's brightness.

next.move: Add the pool light to the lab scene and render its caustics on the vault.

techniques.name: A light well with traced shaft light

thumbnail.alt: The onsen at noon in late August, a hazy beam from the light well falling across the room onto the pool
thumbnail.frame: Onsen view, 12:40 on August 20, 2026 (page clock fixed), reduced motion.

techniques.what: A shaft drilled from the clifftop brings sun into the onsen, and its beam, its sun patch, its skylight and the lit steam share one visibility function.
techniques.how: `bin/coastal_lightwell.py` drills a shaft of 0.42 m radius through 1.67 m of rock, leaning 28° toward the noon sun. `createLightWell` in `light-well.mjs` follows four light paths. The sun's shadow map carries the patch on the floor or the water. Dust and humid air in the beam are single scattering with a forward Henyey–Greenstein phase, marched only inside the shaft's elliptic cylinder, after Wronski. `shaftExitRadiance` path-traces the drilled cylinder on a fixed Halton sequence for the radiance leaving the aperture, and the aperture and the sun patch then light the bath as two small area lights in closed form (`wellIrradianceGLSL`).

files.role: Shaft visibility, the beam, the traced aperture radiance and the area lights.
The drilled shaft and the shadow-only vault.
Masks the steam's sunlight with the shaft's visibility.

limits: The shaft passes 5.5 % of the sky, so outside midday the grotto is darker than an open bath. The beam needs a high sun; the October 16 noon frame shows none, the August 20 frame does.
The two area lights are Lambertian, so the wet rim and the water show no glossy reflection of the aperture.
The beam's scattering sees only the shaft's own visibility, not the bather or the screens.

watchlist.adds: Shades polygonal area lights with rough specular lobes in closed form, so the aperture and the sun patch would gleam on the wet rim and the water instead of only lighting them diffusely.
Computes single scattering with shadows from a shadow map, one slice of rays at a time, so the beam and the steam could show the bather's shadow.

techniques.name: Traced sky and lamp bounce

thumbnail.alt: The renovated office at 23:10, Sirui coding at the L-shaped marble desk, the brass task lamp's warm light bouncing onto the desk, the floor and the bookshelf wall
thumbnail.frame: Study view, 23:10 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: A CPU ray tracer bakes sky visibility and one diffuse bounce into probe cages once, then relights them from the actual sky and lamp powers without tracing again.
techniques.how: `createStaticLightField` builds a triangle BVH over the house's static opaque meshes (`createTriangleBVH`), traces eight cosine-weighted sky rays per primary hit, and stores irradiance as first-order spherical harmonics (`accumulateL1`, `evaluateL1`) in 64 probes, eight per room-sized cage, with octahedral distance moments, after Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan and the probe visibility of Majercik and colleagues. Unit sky and lamp bases let a change of hour recombine the cache with zero rays. The field replaces three.js's ambient terms once; direct light, reflections and refraction stay native. The bake runs in yielded slices and frees its accelerator afterwards. When the renovation moved the rooms, the cages followed: the living room and the gym got cages of their own, 61 of the 64 probes stand in free space, and the living room's washi lantern, whose closed globe had hidden its bulb from the bake's 0.18 m emitter radius, declares a 0.26 m emitter so its bounce is no longer zero.

files.role: Probe cages, the bake and the shader binding.
The triangle BVH and the diffuse quadrature.
Equations, ownership and cost.

limits: Static and one bounce. People, props and swaying plants do not shade it.
Four coefficients lose directional contrast, and sparse probes can leak at thin walls.

watchlist.adds: A basis of twelve lobes on an icosahedron's vertices with close to third-order quality from fewer reads, which would restore the directional contrast four coefficients flatten.
Precomputes, for each receiver, which few probes it can see, so the bounce would stop leaking through thin walls.
Stores multi-bounce glossy light in probes and reprojects it, so the glass, the water and the polished wood would reflect the lit house rather than the environment map.

techniques.name: Horizon-based contact light

thumbnail.alt: The office at 15:00, Sirui at the marble desk, soft contact shadows under the monitors, the laptop, the turntable and the shelves
thumbnail.frame: Study view, 15:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: A visibility buffer computed before the beauty pass darkens only indirect diffuse light near contacts, with the closed-form horizon integral of ground-truth ambient occlusion.
techniques.how: `contact-occlusion.mjs` projects the geometric normal into four fixed view-aligned slices and integrates the cosine-weighted visibility above each slice's two horizons in closed form (`horizonIntegral`), Jimenez and colleagues' inner integral, with at most 32 depth probes per pixel. A 3 × 3 reconstruction keeps neighbours on the same tangent plane (`bilateralWeight`), and the paper's cubic fit adds back the light a pale neighbourhood bounces (`bounceVisibility`). `bindContactLighting` scales only each material's indirect diffuse term, so sunlight, emission and reflections are untouched, and a still composes the same way every time.

files.role: The horizon integral and the edge-aware reconstruction.
The room finish that runs the pass.
Equations, controlled comparisons and cost.
An unlisted comparison page.

limits: Screen-space, so it cannot see hidden or offscreen geometry and overestimates thin occluders.
Four fixed slices keep a directional bias, and there are no bent normals or specular occlusion.

watchlist.adds: Replaces the two horizons with a bitmask of occluded sectors, so light passes behind thin shelves and chair legs and nearby surfaces add one bounce of their colour.

next.move: Specular occlusion and bent normals from the same report (its GTSO), so reflections dim in creases too.

systems.name: Surfaces
systems.summary: The renovation's stone family, computed in the shader from world position: lime plaster on every wall, milky veined marble and travertine, with no texture downloads.

techniques.name: Lime plaster, marble and travertine from noise

thumbnail.alt: The renovated living room in the afternoon, a white U-sofa facing the TV on a plaster media wall, lime-plaster walls, a travertine drum table and an oak floor
thumbnail.frame: Living room view, 16:30 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Walls carry soft clouds and overlapping trowel strokes, the office desk and the kitchen run wandering marble veins, and the tables travertine's bands and pores, all from noise evaluated at each surface point.
techniques.how: `finishPhysicalMaterial` keys a procedural kind by material name and builds every pattern from hashed value noise in world-space metres (`surfaceNoise`), so the scale survives the glTF exports' many UV layouts. Plaster blends soft clouds about a metre across with streaks of noise stretched along three stroke directions whose mix changes from patch to patch, drawn in the three axis planes and weighted by the surface normal, Geiss's triplanar texturing, so a curved vault shows no seam; a faint burnish lowers roughness along the strokes. Marble's veins are the sine of a warped coordinate, the construction of Perlin's image synthesizer, widened and faded with the pixel's footprint so they never shimmer; travertine stacks warm bands and small open pores. Each kind perturbs the normal with Mikkelsen's surface-gradient bump mapping and fades its detail below a pixel.

files.role: The procedural kinds and their bump.
The palette whose material names key the kinds.

limits: Trowel strokes fade once a pixel covers more than about 5 mm of wall, so walls read smooth in the wider views.
The light field's bounce uses base colours, so the patterns do not tint the bounced light.
Stretched value noise rather than an exemplar of real plaster, so close up the strokes are softer and more regular than a hand-trowelled wall.

watchlist.adds: Tiles a small photograph of real lime plaster or marble across any wall without visible repetition, by blending random patches while preserving the photograph's histogram, so close-ups would show real trowel texture.
Oriented noise with exact control of stroke direction and spacing and no loss of contrast, which would let the trowel strokes curve in arcs as a plasterer's do.
Anisotropic noise with a chosen spectrum and built-in filtering, an alternative to stretched value noise that keeps the strokes crisp without shimmer at a distance.

systems.name: Water, air and sky
systems.summary: Two bodies of water with different models, bath steam carried by its own heat, one breeze from the Pacific through the house, and a sun placed by La Jolla's clock.

techniques.name: A Pacific of Gerstner waves

thumbnail.alt: The Pacific from the beach at 16:00, choppy waves in front fading into a smooth, sunlit sea toward the horizon
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera on the beach, 16:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Ten Gerstner waves displace the sea and its normals together, with a wind sea that grows with the breeze, gusty ripples and whitecaps, a lit shoreline and a live mirror of the cliff.
techniques.how: `sampleOcean` in `ocean-spectrum.mjs` sums ten choppy Gerstner components from 24.7 m to 6.1 cm with gravity–capillary dispersion and analytic tangents, after Finch, and keeps the steepness sum under 0.3 so the surface never folds. Each amplitude fades with the pixel's footprint, and the slope energy it loses widens the GGX lobe, a scalar version of Bruneton, Neyret and Holzschuch's transition from geometry to BRDF. Since October 16 the seven shorter components are a wind sea that turns and grows with the coast's breeze under a Pierson–Moskowitz cut (`windSeaScale`), pixel ripples follow the local gusty wind by the Cox–Munk slope law (`rippleScale`), and whitecaps cover Monahan and Ó Muircheartaigh's fraction (`whitecapCoverage`). `createPacific` adds swash, wet sand and lit foam, and `createSeaReflection` renders a mirror with exact water Fresnel.

files.role: Wave components, footprint filtering, the wind sea and the CPU wave sampler.
The sea shader, the swash and the foam.
The planar mirror and its Fresnel.
Equations and evidence.

limits: A sparse authored spectrum on a finite 400 m surface, with no FFT, cascades, bathymetry or weather.
The roughness widening is a scalar isotropic fit, not the paper's anisotropic slope statistics.
Waves run straight through the shore and the rocks; nothing reflects, refracts or breaks.
Close up, the swell components draw a faint diamond pattern on the near water.

watchlist.adds: Keeps procedural waves but makes them respect the terrain's boundary, so swells would slow, turn toward the beach and wrap around the rocks.
Derives whitecap coverage from a wave-deformation criterion that filters with distance, so foam would form where waves steepen without the tenfold exaggeration.
Stores wave amplitude by position, direction and wavelength, so waves could reflect off the cliff and bend around the headlands.
Empirical directional spectra, including a shallow-water spectrum and a swell parameter, to drive an FFT ocean if the spectral-ocean move goes ahead.

techniques.name: A height-field onsen

thumbnail.alt: Sirui soaking in the onsen on a Saturday afternoon, his hands at the water's surface by the rim
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera over the pool, 16:10 on Saturday, August 22, 2026 (page clock fixed), after seven seconds of motion.

techniques.what: The onsen is a 40 × 40 shallow-water height field whose waves carry water between cells, reflect off the rim and the bather, and start from the bather's hand.
techniques.how: `createHeightfieldWater` follows section 2.1 of Chentanez and Müller: staggered heights and face velocities, conservative upwind depth fluxes, pressure from the free-surface gradient and reflecting solid faces, at fixed 1/120 s ticks with CFL subdivision; total volume holds to about 10⁻¹⁴. `measurePoolGeometry` measures the real basin, about 0.127 m deep. `createPoolStroke` drives a slow hand skim, and the palm's submerged velocity relaxes nearby face velocities inside each step, so a resting hand adds no energy. `createOnsenWater` packs elevation, slopes and wet weight into a texture for the pool's material and runs only when the camera can see the pool.

files.role: The conservative shallow-water solver.
The renderer adapter and the palm coupling.
Measures the native basin.
The prescribed hand skim.
Equations, coupling limits and numerical evidence.

limits: Shallow-water waves travel at the wrong speed when their wavelength nears the 12.7 cm depth or is shorter, so the hand's ripples are off.
One-way coupling, with no wet and dry cells, splashes, buoyancy or caustics.

watchlist.adds: Splits each step into shallow-water bulk flow and Airy surface waves, so the hand's short ripples would travel at their true speed in this shallow basin.
Couples a height field to a 3D grid and particles where the surface breaks, for splashes when someone steps in or the spout drips.

next.move: A steady drip from the bamboo spout into the solver at the spout's mouth.

techniques.name: Thermal steam

thumbnail.alt: Bath air over the onsen at noon in late August, the light well's beam showing as a pale shaft through it
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera beside the pool, 12:40 on August 20, 2026 (page clock fixed), reduced motion.

techniques.what: Bath mist is two transported fields, droplet concentration and temperature, rendered with single scattering that composes in order around the glass and the water.
techniques.how: `createSteamDensity` advects an 18³ concentration and temperature field at a fixed 30 Hz with midpoint semi-Lagrangian backtracing, after Stam, and lets warmer cells rise faster, after Fedkiw, Stam and Jensen's separate smoke density and temperature; diffusion and cooling use exact exponential factors, and since October 16 the drift follows the house's share of the coast's breeze (`setWind`). `createSteamVolume` marches up to 40 samples with Beer–Lambert extinction and a Henyey–Greenstein phase (`integrateSteamSamples`, `steamPhase`), after Wronski, and splits each ray once at the nearest glass or water (`steamRayIntervals`) so the gas in front and behind composes in order.

files.role: Concentration and temperature transport.
The single-scattering march and the interface split.
Opaque and nearest-transmissive depth for the split.
Model, light integration and cost.

limits: A prescribed buoyant rise with no pressure solve; semi-Lagrangian transport blurs the field and does not conserve its mass exactly.
Single scattering only, with no shadow from opaque geometry beyond the light well's mask.

watchlist.adds: Advects along forward and backward maps for about the cost of two semi-Lagrangian steps, so the 18³ field would keep its wisps instead of blurring them away.
Synthesizes the turbulence a coarse grid misses with wavelet noise, detail far finer than 18 cells at shader cost.
If the steam ever gains a pressure solve, a reflection at mid-step keeps its swirls far longer than projection alone.

techniques.name: One wind for the coast

thumbnail.alt: The date palm on the clifftop and its shadow on the sand, fronds that sway in the afternoon sea breeze
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera on the clifftop, 15:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: One breeze, measured at Scripps Pier and carried by gust fronts that travel downwind, moves the sea, the clifftop planting, the room plants, the curtains, the steam and the particles.
techniques.how: `createCoastWind` in `wind-field.mjs` runs a periodic cubic Hermite through the October hourly means at Scripps Pier (NDBC LJPC1, 2023–2025) and writes every gust as a function of retarded time t − x·d/c, so a front reaches each place in turn at the mean wind's speed, Taylor's frozen turbulence. An exact integer hash makes the shader chunk (`coastWindGLSL`) and the CPU agree on every gust. Indoors, a six-mode curl-noise field adds the house's own eddies (`sampleWind`), exactly divergence-free, after Bridson, Hourihan and Nordenstam. `patchFloraSway` bends the planting by a lean that grows like U^1.4, as streamlining leaves' drag does, and a sway at each species' own frequency phased by retarded time, so gusts roll across the bluff; the room plants bend around their real stems.

files.role: The daily breeze, the gust fronts, the indoor eddies and the shared GLSL.
The planting's sway and the room plants' rooted bend.
Binds the room plants to the field and the coast's state.
Dust and spray carried by the wind.
The curl field, leaf attachment and particle integration.

limits: Frozen turbulence over flat ground. There is no shelter or speed-up from the bluff, the house or the cliff, and no change with height.
The outdoor field is not divergence-free; only the indoor eddies keep the curl field's guarantee.
October's daily cycle all year.
Trunks and branches stay rigid; only leaves, needles and fronds move.

watchlist.adds: Projects the wind onto a few precomputed modal stresses per tree, so the Torrey pines and the palm would sway as whole structures, evaluated on the GPU.
Precomputes branch responses to turbulent wind in a motion texture read by one vertex shader, so branches would bend by their own stiffness.
Draws grass blades as geometry with gravity, wind and collisions on any surface, so the bluff's grass could part around the rabbits.

next.move: Follow the station's monthly cycles, so summer afternoons blow harder than October's.

techniques.name: Sun position and sky

thumbnail.alt: The sun low over the Pacific at 17:40, a glitter path on the water below a pale, hazy sky
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera on the beach looking west, 17:40 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: The sun, its shadows and the sun's disc follow NOAA's solar equations for La Jolla on the scene's Pacific clock; the sky's colours are authored.
techniques.how: `coastalDaylight` in `daylight.mjs` uses NOAA's fractional-year approximation at 32.83° N, 117.27° W, with Pacific daylight saving. In `environment.mjs`, `setPalette` sets the sky shader's zenith and horizon colours by time of day and points its sun from the daylight model, and `makeEnvironment` captures the sky into a prefiltered environment map at twenty-minute steps with one generator for the home's lifetime. On the coast the sun's shadow map follows the camera, snapped to whole texels. Night's key light is an authored moon.

files.role: Solar position.
The sky shader, its environment captures and the haze.

limits: Not an atmospheric scattering model. The sky's colours and the haze are chosen by hand, so a sunset does not redden by physics.
Reflections can lag the sun within a twenty-minute step, and there is no lunar astronomy.

watchlist.adds: An analytic sky-dome model fitted to radiative-transfer simulations, a few coefficients per colour band, the quickest step to a sky gradient and sunset that follow the sun.
A physically based sky and aerial perspective from small lookup tables, with multiple scattering, cheap per frame, so sunsets and the coast's haze would come from scattering.
Precomputed multiple scattering for every view and sun direction, the method the 2020 work builds on, in case per-frame tables cost too much.

systems.name: Cloth, skin and motion
systems.summary: Fabric that moves in the breeze or drapes over a sleeper, skin and hair that take light like skin and hair, and bodies and animals posed on the house's real geometry.

techniques.name: Sheer curtains in the breeze

thumbnail.alt: The renovated kitchen at 16:45 between two sheer curtain panels, the island, the coffee bar and the round dining table behind them
thumbnail.frame: Kitchen view, 16:45 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion (settled drape).

techniques.what: Four sheer panels inside the glass front, a position-based cloth in the coast's breeze, with a weave whose openness, glow and shadow change with the angle.
techniques.how: `createCurtainCloth` steps 29 × 25 particle panels with small-step extended position-based dynamics: colour-batched structural, shear and bend constraints, long-range tethers, and a kinematic heading of carrier rings whose sine folds gather or spread. Air acts per triangle from the wind relative to the cloth, a flat-plate normal force plus skin friction applied semi-implicitly, and `createFacadeDraft` feeds jets through an open door from the coast's onshore breeze. `weaveOpenness` treats the voile as a plain weave of round yarns, so its gaps close toward grazing angles; back light passes as a thin Lambertian sheet plus a forward Henyey–Greenstein lobe, and a dithered shadow pass leaves a partial pool of light. `createCurtainRig` steps panels on screen at 30 Hz, and `curtainSchedule` draws them against the low sun.

files.role: The cloth solver, the facade draft and the schedule.
Weave openness, transmission and the dithered shadow.
The live scene's curtains and their visibility budget.
Equations, sources, cost and limits ("Curtain cloth").

limits: No self-collision, so gathered stacks can pass through themselves in strong gusts.
The air has no shielding or wake, so a stack's inner folds feel the full wind.
Depth shadow maps cannot colour the light the yarn lets through.
The fabric is authored, not measured; there is no yarn-level or microcylinder model.

watchlist.adds: Shades cloth from its yarn hierarchy with fibre-level reflection and transmission, so the sheer's glow and openness would follow the yarn rather than one cylinder per thread.
Repulsion-based self-collision for cloth on the GPU, so gathered stacks would stop passing through themselves.
Solves the cloth one vertex block at a time with local Newton steps, stable at large time steps, so the panels could keep their stiffness at 30 Hz without XPBD's substeps.

techniques.name: Bedding draped by position-based dynamics

thumbnail.alt: Sirui asleep at 04:00 under a duvet draped over his body, the pillow dented under his head
thumbnail.frame: Sleep view, 04:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Each avatar's duvet is dropped over the sleeping body offline by a position-based cloth solver and its pillow pressed in by the head, so no cover cuts through a chest; in the scene the cover breathes.
techniques.how: `draped_duvet` in `bin/coastal_bedding.py` builds a height field of everything under the cover (`support_field`: sleeper, pillow, mattress, frame and bedside table) and `drape` drops a cloth grid onto it with coloured Gauss–Seidel distance constraints and a soft bend, after Müller and colleagues and Fratarcangeli, Tibaldo and Pellacini; the cover is then trimmed across the chest, quilted and given 3 cm of fill. `sleepers` poses every avatar's sleep clip at its deepest and shallowest breath, and `pillow` presses each pillow wherever a sleeping head rests. `bin/refresh_coastal_bedding.py` rebuilds the six bed variants in the retained house. In the scene, `createBreathingCover` in `bedding-breath.mjs` lifts the sleeper's cover a few millimetres along its normals around the chest at about fourteen breaths a minute, inhaling over 40 % of each breath (`breathAt`).

files.role: The position-based drape and the pressed pillows.
Builds the six variants in the retained house.
Asserts the body, cover and pillow clearances.
The cover's breath in the scene.

limits: The drape is offline. In the scene the cover only breathes, a scripted swell of 7 mm at the chest, so it cannot follow a sleeper who turns.
Contact is against an upper envelope of the bodies, not two-sided collision.
The drape itself has no automated test; the review script records its clearances in `artwork/coastal-home/reviews/bedding.json`.

watchlist.adds: Intersection-free contact for cloth and thin shells, so an offline drape could hold the duvet off every body without the trim and the fill that hide contact today.
The same block-descent solver offline, a stable replacement for the Gauss–Seidel drape that converges in fewer iterations.

techniques.name: Preintegrated skin diffusion

thumbnail.alt: Sirui at his desk in the late afternoon, close up, his face lit softly from the side, the turntable and the bookshelf behind him
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera at the face, 16:40 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Skin spreads direct light across a curved patch with a normalized diffusion profile, so a shadow's edge on the face turns warm instead of hard.
techniques.how: `buildDiffusionTable` in `skin-diffusion-profile.mjs` integrates Christensen and Burley's normalized two-exponential profile over a locally spherical patch (`diffuseResponse`, with 96-node Gauss–Legendre quadrature) into a 257 × 49 half-float table. `createSkinDiffusion` measures mean curvature in metres from view-space derivatives of the skinned surface and replaces only the direct diffuse term of three.js's physical material with a 70/30 mix of diffused and ordinary response (`patchSkinDiffusionShader`). The red, green and blue distances, 3.2, 1.2 and 0.65 mm, are authored, not measured.

files.role: The profile integral and the lookup table.
Curvature and the material hook.
Derivation, integration and limits.

limits: A local convex-sphere approximation with pointwise shadows, so no light crosses a shadow's edge and nothing shines through an ear.
Anisotropic shapes reduce to scalar mean curvature.

watchlist.adds: One-pass screen-space subsurface scattering with variance-guided sampling, so light would cross shadow edges on the face, which a per-point table cannot.

next.move: A spatial, diffuse-only buffer filtered with separable kernels, after Jimenez and colleagues, to carry light across shadow edges.

techniques.name: Strand highlights on hair

thumbnail.alt: Sirui at the desk at night, the desk lamp drawing bright bands across his long black hair
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera at the head, 23:10 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.name: Lifts posed on each figure

thumbnail.alt: Sirui doing pull-ups on the gym's tower at 18:12, hands on the bar, the power cage and the training board beside him

techniques.what: Every lift in Sirui's program is solved each frame on the avatar's own skeleton, so the hands meet the real bar whatever the body's proportions.
techniques.how: `createLiftRig` in `lift-rig.mjs` poses the hips, pelvis, spine and head for each movement, then reaches each hand and foot target with an analytic two-bone solve toward a pole hint (`solveLimb`): knees out over the toes, elbows back on dips. Clearances come from each figure's own head, measured from the skinned bind-pose vertices (`measureHead`), so a bar passes under or behind a cartoon head. Each repetition eases in and out (`lowerThenDrive`, `driveThenLower`), the slow in and slow out that Thomas and Johnston describe and Lasseter carried into 3D animation. `trainingAt` turns the date into the day's nSuns session, `sessionPose` stages it and routes walks around the equipment on a visibility graph (`planRoute`), and `createGymProps` loads the plates and draws the board.

techniques.name: Animals that plant their feet

thumbnail.alt: Two Brandt's cormorants on a rock at the cliff foot, a California sea lion below them and the sea behind
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera 4 m from a cormorant's roost, 15:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Twenty-eight skinned animals, from rabbits and sea lions to brown pelicans and Brandt's cormorants, act in irregular epochs sampled from time, with feet that hold their contacts on the exported terrain, rock and sea.
techniques.how: Each species is one skinned mesh whose bones rest at identity, so backs bend, jaws open and tails, ears, flippers and wingtips follow through; 28 animals draw 56 primitives where 17 rigid-part animals drew 256. The acting is original and sampled from absolute active time, so a pause or a slow frame cannot accumulate drift. Epoch boundaries are jittered (`epochAt`), and posture channels are springs driven by keyed targets (`sprung`): a linear spring's response to stepped targets is the sum of one step response per change, so a turn overshoots and settles without integrating frames. `rabbitActing` holds a rabbit's travel at takeoff and landing and advances it only in the air, `raccoonMotion` keeps stance paws on world anchors while two-joint legs follow (`plantedFoot`), `shorebirdMotion` turns sandpipers at each zero-speed reversal, and `gullMotion` joins flight and perch with transitions continuous in acceleration. Pelicans fly a line a metre above the displaced sea the renderer draws, passing a wave of wingbeats down the line (`pelicanMotion`); `solvePerchLanding` fits each gull's webbed foot to exported perch triangles, and the cormorants stand on exported rock roosts.

Rabbit and marine acting.
Raccoon, sandpiper and gull acting.
The pelican line, its dive and the cormorants.
Gull feet on real perches.
Skinned clones, populations, the off-screen gate and inspection.

Contacts are checked at samples, with no guarantee between them.
Wildlife shaders still compile on a species' first draw rather than in the program warmup.

watchlist.adds: Physics-based quadruped gaits with a flexible spine, so a rabbit's hop or the raccoon's walk would answer slope and landing.
Blends expert controllers learned from quadruped motion capture, for natural transitions between walking, trotting, sitting and standing.
Controls flapping flight from wingbeat data, so the gulls could flap, glide and recover in the coast's gusts.

systems.summary: A camera that knows the house's walls from its own geometry, and land that continues past the mainland in every direction, out to a coast the camera can now see from 160 m.

techniques.name: A camera that knows the house's walls

thumbnail.alt: The cave house in its cliff from far out over the Pacific, with the mesa, its planting and the coast running on into the haze
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera about 155 m out over the sea, 15:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: Every static mesh is voxelized into a 12 cm field once it loads, and a spring arm keeps the camera on the near side of anything between it and the subject, so visitors can orbit freely and zoom the coast to 160 m.
techniques.how: `createCameraField` in `camera-field.mjs` voxelizes each static house, room and coast mesh in a module worker (`camera-field-worker.mjs`), and `camera.mjs` classifies the cells: pieces under 45 cm in every direction are detail, a cell blocks when its neighbourhood holds a plane's worth of structure, and blocking cells grow a 24 cm clearance shell. Rays walk the field cell by cell, after Amanatides and Woo. `cameraArm` places the camera at the farthest point on the orbit ray the path reaches without crossing a blocking cell, with side rays that pull in before an edge reaches it, and `steerOrbit` refuses steps that would leave the arm under 40 % of the requested distance. `farView` lets the haze, the clip planes and the sun's shadow follow the coast's orbit out to 160 m. Since October 18 the gym's camera works like a tripod, turning to each station from its authored place (`tripodLook`), and full screen on a portrait screen widens the lens to hold a room's width (`portraitFov`).

files.role: Voxelizes the loaded meshes and decides what may hold the camera back.
Voxelizes off the main thread.
Classifies the cells, walks rays, steers the arm and frames the gym and portrait screens.

limits: Ready about 3.3 s after the rooms stream in. Characters, P, the animals and the clifftop planting are not in the field.
Nothing scores the composition, and one 40 % threshold serves every room.

A compact camera space built around on-screen subject positions, so a room's framing could be composed rather than only kept clear.

techniques.name: The land beyond the mainland's walls

thumbnail.alt: Sandstone bluffs north of the house cut by a canyon, the gliderport's lawn and Torrey pines on top, and a paraglider overhead
thumbnail.frame: Lab camera about 120 m off the north bluffs, 15:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026, reduced motion.

techniques.what: A terraced mesa with badland canyons, bluffs with the gliderport, a headland with sea caves and a distant point continue the coast past the mainland's flat walls.
techniques.how: `bin/build_coastal_hinterland.py` snaps the new ground to the mainland's 225 back-edge and 41 end-edge vertices (`snap`, `end_edge`) and continues the mainland's own height, cliff and beach functions across each seam, eased over 25 m. One constrained Delaunay triangulation, after Shewchuk's Triangle, runs from 0.5 m triangles at the walls to 18 m on the far hill, with occlusion baked into vertex colours. Planting, trails, the gliderport's lawn and a deck over three sea caves follow photographs of Torrey Pines, Black's Beach, Goldfish Point and the gliderport. `bindHinterland` loads the 1.36 MB model on the first visit outside and merges its terrain into the camera's height grid (`mergeCameraGrid`), and `bindWindsock` turns the gliderport's wind sock with the coast's wind.

The land's height, cliff and beach functions.
The gliderport, the deck and the planting.
Loads the land, merges its camera grid and binds the wind sock.
The exported land.

Shrubs read as mounds within about 20 m.

Amplifies terrain with implicit 3D features, the overhangs and caves a height field cannot hold, so the sea caves and undercut cliffs could belong to the ground itself.

systems.summary: The house drawn in pen while it loads, traced offline from the authored views' geometry and morphed from drawing to drawing as each piece arrives.

techniques.name: A pen sketch while the house loads

thumbnail.alt: Pen strokes drawing the bedroom while the 3D home loads, the bed and its duvet, a plant, the bedside lamp and a tall cupboard
thumbnail.frame: The homepage 4.6 s into loading, at 04:00 on Friday, October 16, 2026 (page clock fixed), reduced motion (each drawing still).

techniques.what: Pen strokes traced offline from geometry buffers draw the sea, the cliff, the cut-away house and the occupied room while the scene loads, then trace the first rendered frame.
techniques.how: `strokesFrom` in `bin/build_loading_sketch.cjs` traces each authored view's object-ID and surface-normal passes, after Saito and Takahashi's geometry buffers: object outlines weighted by how much of the frame each object fills, creases sharper than about 57°, and long straight runs favoured by the structure tensor's coherence. Eight drawings pack into 45 KB. `createSketchEngine` flies strokes on a damped spring (`springStep`), pairs them with their next targets in Hilbert-curve order (`hilbertIndex`) so a morph flows instead of tangling, and lets a resting drawing breathe (`breathDepth`). `createLoadingSketch` hands an OffscreenCanvas to a worker so model parsing never stalls the strokes.

files.role: Traces the drawings from the authored views.
Stroke motion, Hilbert pairing, breathing and edge tracing.
The page side, the worker hand-off and the first-frame trace.
Draws off the main thread.
The packed drawings.

systems.name: Performance
systems.summary: Where the coastal home's frame goes, and what was cut on October 18, 2026. Outside, the frame was bound by three's per-draw work rather than by pixels, so the cuts target uniform uploads, program switches, shadow-map draws and decoding. In three interleaved pairs, script time per outside frame fell from 89.8 to 56.9 ms, draws from 1,554 to 1,292, shadow-map draws from 353 to 91 and program switches from 579 to 173; at the 160 m coast script time fell from 86.9 to 50.7 ms. Measured on one shared Windows laptop (Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, Arc integrated GPU, headless Chromium on ANGLE/D3D11, a 545 × 461 canvas), where other processes used about half the CPU, so draw counts, script time and pixel parity carry the result and frame rates only illustrate it. The next techniques, in priority order, and the WebGPU decision are under Open problems.

techniques.name: Per-pass frame attribution and still parity
techniques.what: Two scripts measure where each frame's time goes and prove when a change leaves a still frame untouched, so every cut below was measured interleaved, never batch against batch.
techniques.how: `bin/measure_coastal_views.cjs` opens the home in a fresh headless browser per run, seeds page randomness, fixes the routine's clock at Friday 13:20 and samples the occupied study, the authored outside view and the 160 m coast for 6 s each. It attributes every WebGL draw to a pass by its viewport (the 2048 px sun shadow, the 384 px sea mirror, the beauty and output passes at the canvas size, the contact prepass), times the script inside the frame callback and, where the browser allows, the GPU with a timer query, and reads process CPU time. Variants run base, work, work, base, and the result is the median of run medians with the range. `bin/compare_coastal_stills.cjs` captures reduced-motion stills in the same order, and the base pair is the control.

files.role: Per-view, per-pass frame cost in interleaved variants.
Pixel parity, base, work, work, base.
How to measure, the results, the rules for later work and the next steps.
The October 18 tables, attribution, parity and decoding runs.

limits: Hiding objects under reduced motion needs a requested frame, or the capture repeats the old frame; the first transmission check reported zero changed pixels for that reason.
Other processes on the shared laptop stretch frame intervals while the page is idle, so frame rates are reported but not relied on.

techniques.name: Vector-array uniforms stored flat
techniques.what: The light installations' and the light field's arrays of vectors are stored as flat Float32Arrays, so three no longer re-flattens them on every material switch, which was the largest single cost of an outside frame.
techniques.how: Three r164 flattens a uniform that is an array of `Vector3` or `Vector4` element by element whenever a material's uniforms upload, and this scene switches material on nearly every draw, because each mesh owns its material. The ten arrays in `createLightInstallations` (4 or 12 vectors each) and the three in `createStaticLightField` cost about 100,000 `Vector3.toArray` calls per outside frame: a CPU profile put 19.9 % of the main thread in `toArray` and 7.9 % in three's `flatten`. As flat typed arrays they pass through untouched, and the GPU receives the same float32 values (the CPU sampler keeps a double-precision copy). With every other change in place, holding these two files back left the outside frame at 80 ms of script against 42 to 47 ms, so this change is what makes the draw grouping and the shadow cache pay off.

files.role: Line and point emitters as flat arrays.
Region bounds and the fallback as flat arrays.

limits: Every draw still refreshes its own material's uniforms; only materials shared between meshes would skip that.

next.move: Share identical materials between meshes, so runs of draws with one material skip three's material refresh. About 35 µs of script remain per outside draw; the expected saving is a further 20 to 40 % of outside script time, in about half a day.
next.why: It touches materials.mjs and realism.mjs, which the renovation owns.

techniques.name: Opaque draws grouped by shader program
techniques.what: Opaque draws that share a shader program run together, which cut program switches in an outside frame from about 580 to 173.
techniques.how: Three r164 sorts opaque draws by material id, and with one material per mesh nearly every draw switched program, each switch re-uploading the camera, the light structs and the material's uniforms. `sortOpaqueByProgram` installs an opaque sort that groups draws by program and ranks each group by the earliest material id that uses it, so groups keep three's old relative order and the sea still draws before the beach, then sorts by material and depth. Against the same build without it, outside script time fell from 59 to 44 ms and the study's from 15.7 to 12.7 ms (two runs each). Only exact depth ties between surfaces of different programs can resolve differently: in matched stills 39 pixels changed outside (at most 40 of 255 in one channel, on the clifftop planting and the glass front's edges), 6 in the study and 4 at 160 m. An unranked first version changed about 340 pixels along the waterline.

files.role: The program-grouped opaque sort.
Installs the sort; `?draw-order=material` restores three's order.
The 39 changed pixels, ringed.

limits: Whether any tie pixel matters is Sirui's call.
Merging static meshes stays rejected, because nearly every mesh is interactive, animated or wind-swayed.

watchlist.adds: Lets three's BatchedMesh draw the hinterland's 156 static primitives and the planting's 23 in a few multi-draw calls with per-object culling, about 100 to 150 fewer draws per pass outside, once each piece's transform is baked into its geometry.
A hierarchical depth test that would skip the rooms hidden behind the cliff and the roof when the camera is out at the coast, where they draw about 130 meshes per pass.
Rasterizes a few large occluders on the CPU into a coarse depth buffer and tests room bounds against it, answering in the same frame instead of a frame late like a GPU query.
Two-phase occlusion culling that reuses last frame's visible set, which would hide the rooms from the coast without the pop-in of a one-frame-late query.
Replaces the far hinterland canopy (82,000 triangles in 19 chunks) and the clifftop flora (184,000) with a few textured planes at distance, cutting triangles where they are smallest on screen.

techniques.name: A cached static sun shadow
techniques.what: Casters that never move are drawn into the 2048 px sun shadow map once and copied in each frame; only moving casters are drawn over the copy.
techniques.how: `createShadowCache` wraps three's shadow pass. Static casters go into a cached map; each frame `blitFramebuffer` copies the cached packed depth and depth buffer into the light's map, and the moving casters are drawn over it without a clear: the two-stage cache of Myers's shadows for Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War, the same split as Unity HDRP's cached shadows and Unreal Engine's virtual shadow map page cache. Movement is observed, not declared: a change of world matrix, geometry, position or index buffer version, draw range or material makes a caster dynamic until it has held still for 30 rendered frames, twice as long each time it moves again (up to 1,800). Skinned, morphing, instanced and batched meshes and casters with their own depth material, such as the swaying planting, always are. The cache is redrawn when the static set changes, when the light or its shadow camera moves (the coast's shadow square follows the camera target in whole texels; the sun follows the clock, checked every 30 s) or when the map is replaced: 12 rebuilds in 1,795 study frames. Shadow-map draws per frame fell from 267 to 37 in the study, 353 to 82 outside and 404 to 91 at the coast. Redrawing the whole map inside a live frame matched the cached map to the texel in 7 of 8 checks; the eighth differed in 1 of 4,194,304 texels, an exact tie between a static and a moving caster.

files.role: Caster classification, the cached map and the per-frame copy.
Installs the cache; `?shadow-cache=0` turns it off, and the lab's check compares it with a full redraw.

limits: Three r164 tests shadow layers against the main camera, so the split toggles `castShadow` around each pass.
A caster animated only in its vertex shader without its own depth material would be cached in place. None exists, and the performance notes make it a rule.

next.move: Cull room casters by the camera's cell, so a room the camera cannot see leaves the moving set.

techniques.name: A shared Draco decoder pool
techniques.what: Every model loader on the page shares one pool of up to four Draco decoder workers, so a model's primitives decode in parallel.
techniques.how: Three's GLTFLoader decodes each Draco primitive as its own task, and one worker per loader serialized them. `createModelLoader` gives every loader on the page (the home, its wildlife, the footer coast) one pool of half the cores, at most four, and ends it when the last loader is disposed. In isolation (eight interleaved rounds, warmed decoders, median) the house shell decoded in 118 ms instead of 323, the avatar in 130 instead of 315, the kitchen in 74 instead of 151 and the hinterland in 180 instead of 388. Because the pool outlives any one load, it must not remember a failure: a failed decoder download is fetched again by the next decode, a failed worker is retired, and a retry after a failed load starts fresh.

files.role: The shared pool, its reference count and its failure handling.

limits: In full cold starts on the loaded laptop the gain disappeared in the noise. Startup is dominated by compiling about 70 shader programs, 12 to 19 s to the first composed frame there.
Decode order now varies, which exposes a race in how reduced-motion wildlife poses compose (2,334 px of animals in different poses, seen in the unchanged base too).

watchlist.adds: Meshopt decoded 3.4 to 7.5 times faster than the four-worker Draco pool here (the house shell in 23 ms instead of 118) at 1 to 46 % more bytes after gzip; it would run as a post-process after the Blender export, with quantization matched to the Draco settings and the planting's custom attributes kept.

techniques.name: A drawing-buffer pixel budget with adaptive density
techniques.what: The drawing buffer is capped at 2.1 megapixels, and a full-screen buffer of a megapixel or more steps its density down only while frames wait on the GPU.
techniques.how: Full screen can ask for 2560 × 1440 CSS pixels at a device pixel ratio of 1.5, about 8.3 MP, where the 4× multisampled half-float composer targets alone take on the order of a gigabyte. `createResolutionGovernor` caps the buffer at `PIXEL_BUDGET` (a 2560 × 1440 screen at DPR 1.5 draws 1920 × 1080). On buffers of 1 MP or more it steps density down by 0.85, to no less than 0.7, only while frames are slow and waiting on the GPU rather than on script; it keeps a step only if the 75th-percentile frame time improves by 10 %, stops after two unhelpful probes, steps back up after three fast seconds and never moves while the scene is still, after Binks's dynamic resolution rendering and the hysteresis of drei's PerformanceMonitor. It scales the logical size handed to the renderer and to the finish composer, never the pixel ratio the composer captured, so every pass stays at the canvas size. In the home's full screen at 2560 × 1440 and DPR 1.5, main drew 3840 × 2160 at 4.4 fps in the study and 2.7 fps outside; with the budget the buffer was 1642 × 923, at 11.9 and 6.1 fps.

files.role: The budget and the adaptive factor.
Feeds the renderer and the composer; `?resolution=fixed` keeps the budget without adaptation.

limits: The ordinary canvas (0.25 to 1 MP) never adapts. Outside frames are bound by draw submission, so fewer pixels would only blur.

watchlist.adds: Temporal antialiasing in place of the 4× multisampled half-float targets would save bandwidth and allow a lower internal resolution, but only with correct motion vectors for the skinned, swaying and cloth meshes.

next.move: When frames are GPU-bound, lower the multisample count before the resolution.
next.why: It changes the composer targets in realism.mjs, a look decision.

next.move: Cap ambient animation at 60 fps on high-refresh displays, keeping the full rate while the visitor drags.
next.why: A smoothness decision, and untestable on this 60 Hz headless setup.

techniques.name: A visibility gate for three's transmission copy
techniques.what: An occlusion-query gate that would have skipped three's opaque copy for refraction whenever no transmissive surface was visible from a held camera pose.
techniques.how: Three redraws every opaque object into a full-size multisampled target whenever a transmissive mesh survives frustum culling (the onsen water, the coffee hopper's glass), about a quarter of an outside frame's draws. In a sweep of 108 coast cameras the onsen water showed from only 21, at 3 to 143 pixels, so hiding it outright was not acceptable. The gate queried the transmissive meshes' padded bounding boxes against the shell, coast and room depth at a pose held still, and used the answer only for that exact pose.

retired.reason: It was correct but never engaged. All 13 queries in a 12-angle sweep said visible, because the padded boxes show between the cedar slats, over the pool rim and through the glass front where the meshes add no pixels, and the damped camera rarely repeats a pose exactly. It was removed before the performance work merged; a non-transmissive stand-in for distant water is the open move.

history.title: Two renderers, one minute
history.frame: I agreed to the Metropolis experiment. Show, on light the house actually has, when Markov chain Monte Carlo beats independent sampling and when it does not.
dimensions: the sun's size against a minute's budget
how much of a visitor's processor the page may use
history.move: A dependency-free renderer of a simplified onsen whose single path sampler is fed independent numbers (path tracing) or mutated ones (Kelemen's Metropolis), raced in module workers on its own page.
history.backtalk: After a minute path tracing was off by 984 % and Metropolis by 180 %. Metropolis's total brightness is itself a rare-event estimate, because the bootstrap usually holds no sun path. Lazily replayed small steps left a few-percent bias until unread coordinates were redrawn, and a slab shortcut created ghost water hits that tests now catch.
history.reframe: The engine is ready for the pool light's caustics, and for manifold-based mutations if the race should be won outright.

history.backtalk: The October noon sun stays below the light well's shaft, so the first light-well still showed no beam and the frame moved to an August noon. Checking the papers caught four DOIs in the draft list that resolved to other papers.
history.reframe: Which paper comes first is Sirui's call; the shortlist puts a visible change in each of light, sky, water and wind.

history.title: Measure the frame, then cut what it actually spends
history.frame: Sirui asked for further optimization of the site and the 3D scene, and for the state of the art to be written down for later models.
history.move: Vector-array uniforms stored flat, opaque draws grouped by program, a cached static sun shadow, one shared Draco pool and a pixel budget for full screen, each measured interleaved against the same tree without it. Outside, script time per frame fell from 89.8 to 56.9 ms and draws from 1,554 to 1,292; the WebGPU question was priced and deferred, and the remaining work was ranked.
history.backtalk: The outside view ran at about 10 fps. Per-pass attribution found four separate costs (three's transmission copy, the sea mirror, the shadow map and per-draw uniform uploads), and a CPU profile found the largest single cost in three's uniform code rather than in draw count. The first transmission check reported zero changed pixels, because hiding objects under reduced motion without requesting a frame re-captured the old frame; a sweep then showed the water from 21 of 108 cameras, and the gate built for it never engaged. A parity run differed by 2,334 px of wildlife, and holding the decoder change back showed the same race in the unchanged base.
history.reframe: Per-draw uniform cost and the sea mirror remain; material sharing, a lighter mirror and a cheaper distant water are next, and the last two need Sirui.

open_problems.title: Which paper first
open_problems.why_hard: Every watchlist entry would make a technique more faithful, but they differ by an order of magnitude in effort and in how much a visitor would notice. The shortlist proposes four with a visible payoff; the choice is a taste call.
candidate_moves: Light paths: specular manifold sampling, to win the race on the caustics outright.
Sun and sky: a scattering sky, for real sunsets and a terrace hour at dusk.
Onsen: dispersive surface waves, so the hand's ripples travel at their true speed.
Wind: a wind projection basis, so the pines and the palm sway as trees.

open_problems.title: Simulation without compute shaders
open_problems.why_hard: The scene renders through WebGL2 and three.js r164, which have no compute shaders. An FFT ocean, a pressure solve for the steam, cloth on the GPU and probe updates all want them, so each must become chains of fragment passes or wait for WebGPU, a move that would touch every material and pass the shader warmup knows. The performance pass priced that move on October 18 and deferred it (open problem "When to move to WebGPU").
candidate_moves: Prototype one FFT pass chain as fragment passes on a separate page and time it against the authored spectrum.
Keep the small solvers (the onsen, the steam, the cloth) on the CPU and move only the ocean's spectrum to the GPU.

open_problems.title: Light that only a tracer can find
open_problems.why_hard: Caustics on the onsen's floor and vault, glossy reflections of the lit house and light through the sheer all follow paths a rasterizer cannot aim at. The light lab finds them on the CPU, but the house has no runtime tracer, and WebGL offers no ray queries.
candidate_moves: Precompute a caustic pattern in the lab and project it in the onsen, moved by the solver's slopes.
Shade the light well's aperture with glossy area lights, the cheapest specular path the house is missing.

open_problems.title: Where the frame still goes
open_problems.why_hard: Outside, the frame is still bound by three's per-draw path. After the October 18 cuts about 800 draws go to the view and three's transmission copy and about 400 to the sea mirror, and each draw refreshes its own material, about 35 µs of script per draw. The three largest remaining savings change pixels or touch the renovation's materials, so they need Sirui; the rest are engineering. The moves are in priority order, with the expected win and the effort for one agent estimated from these measurements.
candidate_moves: Share identical materials between meshes, so grouped draws skip three's material refresh; a further 20 to 40 % of outside script time, in half a day (needs a decision on materials.mjs and realism.mjs).

A non-transmissive stand-in for the hopper glass and the distant onsen water, which removes three's transmission copy outside, about a quarter of the frame's draws, in hours (a look change of a few dozen pixels).
A lighter sea mirror, without interiors or redrawn every other frame while the camera is still; up to half its ~400 draws, in hours (13 of 108 sampled stills changed, median 126 px).
BatchedMesh with multi-draw for the hinterland's 156 static primitives and the planting's 23, with each piece's transform baked into its geometry; 100 to 150 fewer draws per pass outside, in a day.

Meshopt instead of Draco as a post-process, with quantization matched to the Draco settings and custom attributes kept (the default prune strips the planting's TEXCOORD_0 and COLOR_1); about 0.3 to 0.5 s less decoding on a first view for about 0.9 MB more, in half a day.

Minify the ES modules, which jekyll-terser skips; the 3D modules would go from 330 to 201 KB gzipped and the site's other 31 from 110 to 72 KB, in hours, keeping `bin/profile_coastal_startup.cjs` able to find the frame callback.
A content-hashed Service Worker cache, because GitHub Pages serves every file with max-age=600 and re-sends about 10 MB of unchanged models after each deploy; a day.

Room-level occlusion culling from the coast, by one-frame-late queries with hysteresis, two-phase culling or a CPU depth test against real room hulls; up to 130 draws per pass, in two to three days (pop-in while moving needs a decision).
Level of detail for distant planting, simplified chunks with `THREE.LOD` and then impostors; a large triangle cut at distance, in one to two days and three to five for impostors.

Shader compile time at startup (about 70 programs, 12 to 19 s to the first frame on the loaded laptop); measure each program's compile cost, then fewer variants or explicit-level texture reads in the light field's probe loops; possibly seconds, after one to two days of investigation.
Temporal antialiasing instead of 4× multisampled half-float targets, practical only with correct motion vectors for skinned, swaying and cloth meshes, most easily under WebGPURenderer's TRAA node.
Cap ambient animation at 60 fps on high-refresh displays, keeping the full rate while the visitor drags; an hour (a smoothness decision).

open_problems.title: When to move to WebGPU
open_problems.why_hard: Not now. Three.js r186 (September 24, 2026) still calls WebGPURenderer experimental and recommends WebGLRenderer for pure WebGL 2 applications, and WebGPURenderer runs neither `onBeforeCompile` patches, ShaderMaterial nor EffectComposer passes. Every string-patched material here (the procedural kinds, the light field, contact lighting, skin diffusion, the light installations, the light well, the plant and ocean displacement) and the contact, bloom and output passes would be rewritten in TSL. Three.js issue 30560, open since February 2025, reports WebGPURenderer's per-object uniform buffers running several times slower than WebGLRenderer with many distinct objects (about 60 against 15 fps for 20,000 cubes), which is this scene's profile, and a September 2026 comment there measured its WebGL 2 fallback on r186 at 31 % more render CPU and 80 % more GL calls in a draw-heavy app. WebGPU ships in Chrome on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS since 113, on Android since 121 and on Linux from 144, in Safari 26 and in Firefox 141 on Windows, then on Apple-silicon macOS; everyone else would get the WebGL 2 backend. What it would buy here is render bundles that replay static draws without per-draw script, and compute-driven culling with indirect draws, both aimed at the per-draw cost this scene is bound by.
candidate_moves: Wait until issue 30560 is resolved, so WebGPURenderer is at least level with WebGLRenderer on about a thousand distinct draws.
First move the scene from r164 to a current three.js on WebGLRenderer, itself a project, because r182 to r186 rewrote the shadow and BRDF chunks the string patches target.

Then port the materials one at a time to node materials and TSL under WebGLRenderer's NodeMaterial compatibility layer (r184), and switch renderers only if an A/B wins on both the WebGPU and the WebGL 2 backend; several weeks of focused work.
Until then, attack the same per-draw cost on WebGL 2 with material sharing, batching and a lighter mirror.
